title: Why big bands give saxophonists few choruses
summary: Waters says dance and big bands limit solo space, using Lockjaw leaving Basie, Procope with Kirby and Hodges, and his own place in Fletcher's band as examples.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Well, I could improvise, I always could improvise. I mean I knew harmony from, just from natural ability, I always could improvise. See, that's why I didn't like to - I was glad to be with this band because I had a chance to, more so than with my brother, all those dance bands. Dance band is commercial gig, you just play the music where it is and you get paid, but I mean, even big bands you don't - even big bands, that's, I'm sure of this, but I'm pretty sure a lot of these fine saxophonists, jazz men who left these big bands - well, it's like Lockjaw and so forth left the Count Basie before Count Basie retired, I mean I'm sure that you get kinda tired of playing that music, because you don't get as much choruses. You play 16 bars, then you cut off with something else, you know what I mean? That's what I found when I was working in the big bands, you know. The only reason I took the advantage with Fletcher's band, because I took Coleman Hawkins' place. And Coleman Hawkins was a star, way ahead, and every

number had something there for tenor, see. But otherwise you don't get a chance to play. That's why Procope went back musically, I mean as far as choruses are concerned, on his horns. Procope was a great saxophone player then, on the period he was working with Kirby, you understand? But when he worked with these big bands playing first, he didn't get the chance, there was too many others. When this is, like Johnny Hodg[es] and those guys, they would favor them, see, so he didn't have a chance to play as much. So finally after years and years and years you go back, see?
